ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Hydro-power potential in North Eastern States 
*141. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that North Eastern States have large hydroelectric 
power potential; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that out of this potential only one per cent 
thereof has been developed to generate power; and 
(d) whether Government have any immediate plan to exploit the total 
hydro-electric power potential of the No rth Eastern States and make these 
States not only self-sufficient but also a source of revenue for these States? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) to (d) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) On the direction of the Ministry of Power, the Central Electricity 
Authority (CEA) has recently completed a Ranking Study of 399 schemes 
covering all- the river basins in the country. The B^hmaputra and other river 
basins in the North East account for 145 schemes which have been ranked in 
three categories in terms of their attractiveness. Out of these, 41 schemes with 
an assessed potential of 5718 MW have been ranked in the first category and 
86 schemes having an assessed potential of 41,203 MW in the second 
category. This study would enable the potential developers to undertake 
detailed survey and investigation and execution of the viable schemes 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2002] 
in a phased manner. CEA is holding State-wise discussions with the States to 
draw up an action plan for development of the identified hydro power 
projects. 
Government of India is according high priority for development of hydro-
electric projects in the country especi ally in the North-Eastern Region. The 
hydro-electric potential of the North-Eastern States has been assessed at 58,971 
MW which accounts for 38% of the country's total assessed potential. 927 MW 
of this potential has been developed so far. North-Eastern Electric Power 
Corporation (NEEPCO) has recently commissioned Doyang Hydro-electric 
Project (75 MW) in Nagaland and 2 units (270 MW) of the Ranganadi Hydro-
electric Project of 405 MW (3x135 MW) in Arunachal Pradesh. Central 
Power Sector Undertakings have initiated action on a number of new hydro-
electric projects in the North East and Sikkim. National Hydro-electric Power 
Corporation (NHPC) is executing Tccsta Hydro-electric Project Stagc-V (510 
MW) in Sikkim and carrying out prc-constniction activities in . Subansiri 
Lower (2000 MW) in Arunachal Pradesh. NEEPCO is presently executing 
Turial Hydroelectric Project (60 MW) in Mizoram and Kopili (25 MW) 
Hydroelectric Project in Assam. They have also commenced prc-construction 
activities on Kameng Hydro-electric Project (600 MW) in Arunachal Pradesh. 
The harnessing of hydro- electric potential in the North-Eastern Region 
will not only help the States in the region in meeting their requirement of 
power but will also enable sale of surplus power outside the region. 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: Mr. Chairman Si r, it has been stated in the 
reply that the hydro-electric potential of  the North-Eastern States has been 
assessed at 58,971 MW which accounts for 38% of the country's total 
assessed potential. Out of this, hydro-electric potential of only 927 MW has 
been developed so far. It means that hardly 1.5% of the total potential has been 
developed so far. Sir, the development of North Eastern States is required to be 
accelerated for strategic reasons. Besides, the problems of poverty, 
unemployment among the youths, etc. need to be properly addressed. Only 
then, would be able to curb the militancy there. My question to the hon. Minister 
is:  why  is the  hydro-electric potential  of North-Eastern 

[13 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
States not being exploited fully? If it is exploited fully, it would not only help 
in solving the problems of militancy, unemployment, area development, 
prevailing in the North-Eastern States, but would also help in generating 
revenue for those States. It would also help in solving the problem of-power 
shortage in some other States of Indi a like Assam, Bihar, West Bengal, and 
even of Bangladesh. I  would like to know from the hon. Minister as to why 
he is not doing that. What are the constraints? 
SHRI SURESH PRABHU: Mr. Chairman , Sir, I must thank the hon. 
Member for putting a very important questio n. In fact, it tea f act that there is 
a huge hydro potential which is lying untapped in the North-Eastern Region 
of the country, and only less than 2% of the total potential has so far been 
exploited. Therefore, it engaged our attention, and, in fact, I directed the 
Central Electricity Authority to conduct ranking studies of 399 projects 
countrywide to ascertain as to how these projects could be implemented. An 
expert group was constituted to conduc t these ranking studies. We consulted 
several stakeholders and organisations that would be interested in these 
projects. I am very happy to announce that the Central Electricity Authority 
completed this task in a record time. Now, we have got the ranking studies of 
399 projects on all the six river basins in the country including 
Brahmaputra—a huge hydro-electric potential lies in that basin of the North-
Eastern Region. And, now, we have also started holding extensive 
consultations with all the States. In fact, I personally visited all the North-
Eastern States between 1st and 4th of this month, and held extensive 
consultations with the Chief Minister s of the North-Eastern States, and 
whenever it was not possible, with the Governor. We are'at a very advanced 
stage of exploiting this potential fully. As regards the other constraints which 
the hon. Member has mentioned, it is absolutely correct that there is not 
much demand for power in that region. Therefore, most of the power that will 
be generated,, will have to be expo rted outside that region. Therefore, 
transmission network to evacuate the su rplus power will have to be put in 
place. 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: But when would that be done? 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Let him complete. 
SHRI SURESH PRABHU: Simultaneously, we are in the process 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2002] 
of creating the evacuation network, and that plan is also underway. The hon. 
Member, as also the House, must be aware that there is a real technical problem, 
because there is a chicken-neck area through which you have to evacuate all the 
power, and not only just the powerlines, but also other networks like telecom 
network, etc. The other networks have to be passed only through that chicken-
neck area. But, despite that, we are making all possible efforts, and I am vary 
happy to say that, for the first time, we have got a very exhaustive, extensive 
and a very comprehensive plan to deal with the problem of development of power 
in the North-Eastern region as well as to evacuate it from th ere and sell it all 
over the country. 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: Sir, my second supplementary is this. The Minister 
has said that the 399 projects that have been earmarked, win be completed. But I 
would like to put a very specific question to the hon. Minister. What b the number 
of power projects that are likely to be executed in the Tenth Five Year Plan in the 
North-Eastern States? Will the North-Eastern States be surplus with the execution 
of these power projects? If that is so, what will the Government do? How will it 
evacuate the power? Do you have any mechanism in place to evacuate this power, 
and will this power generation eliminate the unemployment problem in the 
North-Eastern States? Sir, the unemployment problem is the main reason for 
militancy in the North-Eastern States? Can you give me some specific time-limit? 
Can you tell me what are the projects that the Government is going to complete in 
the Tenth Five Year Plan, and how these can be linked to development, 
particularly, in eliminating the unemployment problem? How many jobs will you 
create? ....(Interruptions)... From where will you generate resources to execute 
these projects? 
SHRI SURESH PRABHU: Sir, first of a ll, I would like to say that it is 
absolutely a fact that we have not been able to develop substantial projects in 
the North-Eastern region, because there is some insurgency problem. But, 
again, the root cause of the insurgency  problem is also the lack of socio-
economic development of the region. Sir, one problem leads to another 
problem. Therefore, the Government has taken a conscious decision of fully 
exploiting the potential in that region, which will also create...(Interruptions)... 
4 

[13 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
MISS MABEL REBELLO: But when? I want to know what is the exact  time-
frame  within  which  the  Government will  exploit  this 
potential. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: That is all right. 
SHRI SURESH PRABHU: Sir, now we are in the process of fully developing 
it, which will create great employment opportunities in the project itself as well 
as several opportunities downstream, in the tertiary sectors like transportation and 
others, will be created. We are really in the process of doing that. Sir, for the Tenth 
Plan, we are in the process of 4 cvcloP'ng several projects. In Assam, we are 
developing three; in Meghalaya, we are in the processing of adding three; in 
Mizoram, we are developing two; in Sikkim, we are thinking of developing one; 
in Tripura, we are developing one; and, in the Tenth Plan itself, there is a 
possibility of adding one in Assam, with the help of the private sector. The 
NEEPCO has already undertaken some of these projects. The NHPC is also 
developing a project called 'Teesta-V’ in Sikkim. Hopefully, all these projects 
should be completed in the Tenth Plan. At the same time, we are also in the 
process of identifying new opportunities so that all the entire potential could be 
fully exploited. I have already answered the other question, we have already got a 
plan to evacuate the extra power that would be generated in that region, and which is 
not consumed in that region', to the rest of the country, and, if possible, also to 
other countries. Sir, we have also adopted a new strategy. While I waa visiting 
the North-Eastern region at the beginning of this month, ! had directed the 
NEEPCO to look for other opportunities. For example, while we develop 
these major projects of 500 MW, 1000 MW and more, it is also necessary to 
develop mini-hydro and microhydro projects. For that, we are trying to find out, in 
respect of each of the State, what is th e mini-hydro potential. We are in the 
process of discussing all these projects with all the States. We will be holding a 
meeting. I will also personally go there again in the month of April. We will have 
a meeting of all the Chief Ministers to find out as to whether we can exploit the 
potential for the mini-hydro projects within the region itself. And, that particular 
project will also be linked to the village electrification programme, because, in the 
North-Eastern  region,   there  are  some  villages  which  are  yet  to  be 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2002] 
electrified. So, maybe, rather than transmitting power from a far away region, 
these mini-hydro projects can be linked to a nearby village which has to be 
electrified. So, as a part of that package, we are also looking for an 
opportunity as to whether we can also allow the local community to take over 
the distribution of power so that the distribution losses which are creating a 
major 'problem for the country can be  eliminated by involving the local 
community itself. So, this is the overa ll, comprehensive approach that we are 
adopting for power development in the North-Eastern region.

SHRI S.B. CHAVAN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the question which the 
hon. Member has put is a very important one. I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister what is the total potential which is now available in the North-
Eastern States. One of the reasons why the militancy has spread all over the 
North-East is the lack of socioeconomic development of that area. A number 
of schemes have been mentioned here, but there is hardly anything concrete 
in them. Of course, all kinds of scheme s are there, but, I don't think, the 
North-Eastern States will be able to raise the resources. Electricity is the 
important infrastructure which can provide a tremendous volume of 
employment. That can attract not only the National Hydro-Electric Power 
Corporation but the World Bank also. Why shouldn't the World Bank assist 
such a scheme which can, in fact, utilise the huge hydro-electric potential for 
development, not only in the North East but all over the country also? It is 
not a new source of income alone. Automatically, you get water also. The 
only point to which the World Bank can possibly object, is the rehabilitation 
part. So far as rehabilitation is concerned, at least, I have no doubt in my 
mind that you have to satisfy the people who are going to be the sufferers 
due to the submergence of their cultivable land. You should have some kind 
of legislation at the Centre. You request the State Governments also to adopt 
the same so- that the question of rehabilitation does not come in the way. The 
real relief has to be provided to all those re-settlers. If it is attempted in a big 
way, I am sure, the World Bank will also come forward to assist. At the 
international level, there are various other financial agencies which can also 
be attracted for exploitation of such a huge amount of hydro-electric 
potential which is now available in the North-Eastern States. 
SHRI SURESH PRABHU: Sir, the hon. Member is absolutely right 
in saying that we have to find various  ways of raising resources for the 
development of the hydro potential. The Central Electricity

(d) A Statement is laid on the Tabic of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The Defence industry sector has been opened for participation by 
Indian Private Sector upto 100% of equity with Foreign Direct Investment 
(FDI) component of it being permissible upto 26%, both being subject to 
licensing permissions. This includes all types of defence equipment. 
Guidelines have been issued by the Department of Industrial Policy and 
Promotion in consultation with the Ministry of Defence regarding the 
modalities for consideration of applications for grant of licence. The private

partnership   firm   amongst 
17

themselves. The Chief Executive of the company/partnership will be a 
resident Indian. The company/partnership firm can have Foreign Direct 
Investment upto 26% of the equity. Preference would be given to original 
equipment manufacturers or design establishments and those having a good 
track record of supplies. However, there would be a three year lock-in period 
for transfer of equity from one foreign investor to another foreign investor 
and such transfer would be subject to prior approval of the Foreign 
Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) and the Government.

Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion in consultation with the 
Ministry of Defence and the Licences would be granted by the Department of

adequate safety and security procedures which would be subject to 
verification by authorized Government agencies. The quality of the product 
will be assured by the Quality Assurance Agencies of the Ministry of 
Defence.

sector enterprises.

†*153. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': Will the Minister of NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that use of solar energy is far less in comparison to 
the capacity available; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps Government arc taking to popularize the solar energy in 
the country? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
26 

[13 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF NON-
CONVENTIONAL ENERGY SOURCES (SHRI M. KANNAPPAN): (a) to 
(c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Solar energy can be used through two principal routes: the 
thermal route and the photovoltaic route. Both routes arc relevant and 
important for India. The Indian programme on solar energy is one of the 
largest national programmes in the world. A number of solar devices have 
been developed for different applicatio ns and are being installed all over the 
country. A total of around 3,89,000 solar lanterns, 1,84,000 home lighting 
systems. 40,000 street lights, 4,370 water pumps, 6,00,000 sq. meters of 
collector area foj water heating, 5,18,000 solar cookers and 3.1 MW capacity 
of power plants have so far been installed in the country. Nevertheless, it is 
true that the use of solar energy so far in the country is very small in relation 
to the potential for this. The major reasons for this are: 
(i) Solar energy is a highly dispersed resource and is available in day 
time only. Its use requires efficient devices, many with provision to 
store energy for use at nights. 
(ii) The initial cost of most solar devices is high compared to 
conventional energy devices. This acts as deterrent to users despite 
many solar products being competitive on a life cycle basis. 
(iii) Lack of awareness among various categories of users. 
(iv) Inadequate infrastructure for the distribution, sales and servicing of 
solar energy products. 
(c) The Ministry is implementing several programmes to promote 
awareness and to support the use of various solar energy devices in the 
country by providing fiscal and financial incentives like subsidy, soft loans, 
100% accelerated depreciation, concessional duty imports 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2002] 
and excise duty exemption on certain  devices and systems. The following 
steps have been taken in recent years to popularize the use of solar energy: 
(i) Soft loan schemes have been introduced for solar thermal systems 
through the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency 
(IREDA) and some banks. 
(ii) A soft loan scheme for supporting photovoltaic manufacturing 
activities has been introduced. 
(iii) Higher levels of subsidy arc being provided to users in the North-
Eastern States. 
(iv) Special demonstration projects in new application areas and for 
developing new markets arc being funded through grants. 
(v) A model building bye-law for making solar assisted water heating 
systems mandatory in several categories of buildings has been 
drafted and circulated to all State Governments. 
(vi) A demonstration scheme for in stallation of concentrating solar 
cookers in community kitchens is being implemented. 
(vii) Solar power plants and home lighting systems are being used to 
electrify villages in remote areas. 
(viii) A scheme on Establishment of Aditya Solar Shops for making solar 
products available in major cities of the country is in operation. 
(ix) The Ministry has been carrying out publicity and awarencsss 
promotion through advertisements, brochures, exhibitions, mobile 
vans and electronic media. 
(x) R & D projects aimed at improving the efficiency, reliability and 
Economics of solar products are being supported.

Policy regarding private sector participation in power generation 
*155. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) what is the long term planning of the Government with regard to 
power generation in the country through the participation of private sector; 
(b) whether any policy has been laid down in this regard and if so, the 
salient features of the policy; 
(c) whether Government is contemplating to allow Naphtha based power 
projects in the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
38 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 [13 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) A policy 
to encourage greater private sector part icipation in the Indian Power Sector 
was announced in October, 1991. The main objective of this policy was to 
bring in additionality of resources in view of the growing gap between the 
demand and supply of power and the serious resource crunch being faced by 
the State Electricity Boards and Central/State Sector Generating 
Corporations. The policy wa s also expected to raise levels of efficiency, 
productivity and competition. To meet the goal of 'Power on Demand' by 
2012, it is estima ted that an additional capacity of around 1,00,000 MW 
would be required to be set up. Both the private sector as well as Central 
Sector/State Sector will have to contribute towards achieving this target. A 
framework is now available facilitating-private investment in generation, 
transmission and distribution. A regulatory framework has also been set up 
to determine tariffs and provide a level playing field to the private investors. 
(b) The salient features of the priv ate power policy, announced in 1991 
and reviewed from time to time are as under:—  
(i) Private Sector can set up power projects of any size and any type 
thermal projects on conventional fuel, Hydel projects or non-
conventional based on wind/solar energy. 
(ii) Debt equity ratio up to 4:1 allowed. 
(iii) 100% foreign equity partic ipation allowed in generation, 
transmission and distribution. 
(iv) Liberalized rates of depreciation in respect of assets. 
(v) Import of equipment for power projects at concessional customs 
duty. 
(vi) 16% rate of return on equity has been provided. For the portion of 
foreign equity, the return up to 16% can be designated in foreign 
currency to protect it from foreign exchange fluctuations. 
Additional incentive of upto 0.7% can be allowed on each degree 
increase in the normative PLF beyond 68.5%. 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2002] 
(vii) Generating companies can sell power on the basis of a suitably 
structured two part tariff-one part to cover fixed costs and the other 
to cover variable costs at a prescribed level of performance. 
(viii) Guidelines also issued for tariff based competitive bidding 
(availability based tariff) for thermal power stations. 
(ix) Development of captive coal mines permitted as per guidelines of 
Ministry of Coal in this regard. 
(x) Award of power projects, with a few exceptions, through 
International Competitive Bidding (ICB) route made mandatory 
from  18.2.1995 onwards. 
(xi) Powers for grant of environmental clearance decentralized to the 
extent feasible. 
(xii) Capital cost limits exceeding which tcchno-cconomi c clearance is 
required from the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), raised 
suitably. 
(xiii) Automatic approval for foreign investment without any upper limit. 
(xiv) Relaxation of 40% cap on debt exposure by Indian Financial 
Institutions. 
(c) and (d) Naphtha is one of the liquid fuels permitted for use in the 
generation of electricity. Allocation of naphtha to various States has been 
fixed at 12,000 MW. Though a few projects has been commissioned using 
naphtha as a feed stock, naphtha is no longer considered a viable fuel for 
generation of electricity due to its high cost in the international markets and 
difficulty of handling.

Underground mines: 
(i) Introduction of SDLs, LHDs and Continuous Miners wherever possible 
to replace manual loading, thus reducing the concentration of the 
workmen at the working place. 
(ii) Adoption of Roof Bolting in all the workings in large scale for 
support of workings including the areas where roof has been freshly 
exposed. 
(iii) Introduction of man-riding system for travel of workmen in mines 
where lengthy and arduous travelling is involved thus reducing the 
tendency of workmen for set riding. 
(iv) Establishing travelling roadways with shortest possible route in intake 
air-ways with good lighting arrangement. 
(v) Side bolting in the mines where the tendency for the side falls is 
more. 
(vi) Involving scientific institutions  for development of suitable support 
system for the workings. 
Opencast mines: 
(i) Constructing two way haul roads to prevent accidents of dumpers. 
(ii) Constructing haul roads with mild gradient of around 1 in 20 and 
flatter. 
(iii) Strict implementation of traffic rules. 
(iv) Establishing wider benches as far as possible for smooth and safe 
operation of HEMM in excavation areas. 
(v) Keeping optimum bench height suitable to the shovels deployed and to 
the prevailing strata conditions. 
(vi) Introduction of good lighting ar rangements at working place, haul 
roads and dump yards. 
(vii) Providing all workmen with uniforms and helmets with flourcscent 
bands for identification in the dark. 
(viii) Imparting intensive and practical training to contractors' workers.

Effect of new tariff order of CERC 
1129. PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARAT I RAY: Will the Minister of 
POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are awar e of the fact that with the 
implementation of new tariff order of Central Electricity Regulatory 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2002] 
Commission (CERC), investment from the States, Sector in power would be 
seriously affected and will have its impact on NTPC's realization from SEBs; 
(b) whether Government arc also awar e that SEBs would be losing Rs. 
2,300 crore annually after the implementation of CERC orders whereas 
NTPC is expected to bear a loss of about Rs. 2000 crore a year; and 
(c) if so, reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) The Government of India 
constituted the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) and the 
Electricity Regulatory Commissions (ERC) Act, 1989. The functions of 
CERC inter alia include regulation of tariff of generating companies owned 
or controlled by the Central Government and promotion of completion, 
efficiency and economy in  the activities of the el ectricity industry. The 
Central Commission while determining the terms and conditions for fixation 
of tariff is guided by the principle inter alia that generating companies may 
earn an adequate return and at the same time they do not exploit their 
dominant position in generation, sale of electricity. 
The Central Government deleted the provisions of Section 43A(2) of the 
Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 with effect from 15th May, 1999 in exercise 
of powers under Section 51 of the ERC Act, 1998. The Government of India 
had informed CERC in June 1999 that while regulating tariff they would be 
free to depart from the norms fixed vide the 1992 tariff notification. 
CERC issued orders on 4.1.2000, 15.12.2000, 21.12.2000 on Availability 
Based Tariff (ABT) and Tariff PrincipIcs /Norms. In addition to being a 
performance based tariff for the supply of power by Central generating 
stations, the ABT is aimed at incentivising maintenance of grid discipline. By 
these orders CERC revised the norms fixed by the Central Government in the 
tariff notification of 1992. National Th ermal Power Corporation (NTPC) has 
estimated a reduction in revenue to the tunc of Rs. 981 crore in the current 
financial year due to the orders of the CERC. 
CERC has also allowed NTPC to charge 5% of capacity charge in 
112 

[13 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
every bill as development surcharge to meet the requirement of funds for 
enhanced capacity addition. NTPC ha s not taken into account the earning 
which it would get from this surcharge while estimating the reduction in 
revenue. 
Any reduction of tariff due to enhanced efficiency norms will benefit the 
SEBs. Loss to SEBs can come from th e unscheduled interchanges (UI) 
charges, which are leviable in the event of failure of SEB to maintain grid 
discipline. If SEBs maintain grid discip line, they will not be required to pay 
UI charges.

Uniform national policy on drinking water in rural areas 
1150.  SHRI DARA SINGH CHAUHAN: 
SHRIMATI GURCHARAN KAUR: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government propose to evolve a uniform national policy 
on drinking water in rural areas; 
(b) if so, by when; and 
(c) if not, the reasons thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (c) Drinking 
Water Supply being a State subject, the schemes for providing drinking 
water supply in rural areas arc implem ented by the State Governments with 
their own resources. The Government of India supplements the efforts of the 
States by providing funds under th e Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP) and the Rural Drinking Water component of the 
Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY). The State Governments have 
the powers to plan, sanction and implement individual rural drinking water

been fully covered and 1,46,674 have been covered partially covered with 
drinking water supply facilities. Only 17,710 habitations still remain to be 
covered with drinking water supply facilities. 
National Agenda for Governance of the Government envisages coverage 
of all the rural habitations with drinki ng water facility by the year 2004. As 
such, there is no proposal to evolve a national policy exclusively on drinking 
water in rural areas.

V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The new Order has made 
the Government machinery more industry friendly and less obstrusivc. 
The salient features of the new order arc as follows:—  
• presentation of the material has been simplified making for easier 
comprehension; 
• procedures of filing of Informa tion Memoranda on installation of 
machines in respect of spinning, knitting and powerloom sectors have

office of Textile Commissioner has been removed;

retained so that he may discharge his responsibility in respect of hank 
yarn obligation order, reverse twist order, Olive green shade and 
marking on textiles. It has also been made clear that the Textile 
Commissioner can now insist on markings on the imported textile 
articles also. 
• Keeping in view the inadequacy of regulatory machinery available with 
the Textile Commissioner, powers of the Textile Commissioner to 
control production and supply have been diluted by and large. With a 
view to protecting the industrial units from possible harassment by 
inspectors, it has been provided th at powers of search and seizure

textile manufacturers.

1158. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased

of EU; Canada) has been governed by bilateral textile agreements entered 
into between India and these countrie s under the aegis of the Multi-Fibre 
Arrangement (MFA). outside the rules of the General Agreement on Tariffs 
and Trade (GATT). With effect from  January 1, 1995, the quantitative 
restrictions (import quotas) in the bilateral agreements under the MFA, arc 
being governed by the Agreement on . Textiles and Clothing (ATC) 
contained in the Final Act of the Uruguay Round negotiations of the GATT.

foreign exchange earners has started picking up by the end of January 2002;

industry has started looking up, as th e production of textiles in January 2002

(d) and (e) According to the latest  available information exports of 
readymade garments in physical terms since January 2002 has shown a 6%

50,000 shuttleless looms and to modernise 2.5 lakh powerlooms in the

SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL (Nominat ed): Sir, Delhi is afflicted

SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN (Kerala): Sir, the Kerala Minerals and 
Metals Ltd. and Chavara and Tr avancore Titanium Products, 
Thirunanthapuram, are two prestigiou s State-owned public sector 
undertakings engaged in the producti on of Titanium Dioxide pignment, and 
have been running in profit, continuous ly, for the last so many years. The 
import duty on Titanium Dioxide pigment, during the year 1985, was 135 per 
cent, and the basic price of the pigment  was nearly Rs. 1,30,000/- per MT. 
The Government of India, through it s Budgets, later on, reduced the import 
duty, which now stands at 35 per cent. As a result of the steep decline in the 
import duty on Titanium Dioxide, the foreign manufacturers are dumping their 
products in India and selling it product at a lower rate. 
It is a clear case of dumping wh ich is against the spirit of 
international market and trading. As a result of this, the stock of titanium 
dioxide in the KMML and the TTP has increased to a record high and they are 
forced to sell the product at the rate of Rs. 90,000 per tonne endangering the 
future prospects of the indigenous industry. Therefore, any change in the 
present import duty on the titanium dioxide pigment would perish the domestic 
industry, which otherwise has a very bright future. 
Therefore, it is requested that t he import duty on titanium dioxide 
should not be reduced further. The pres ent level of import duty on titanium 
dioxide should  be maintained.

DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY (Nominated ): Mr. Chairman Sir, I seek 
your kind permission to refer to an impor tant issue that needs special attention 
of the august House. The increasing nu mber of television channels has been 
prompting enterprising persons to be come cable T.V. operators. If their 
transactions are fair, no doubt, they will be rendering real service to the people.

country, several cable T.V. operators are virtually behaving like a mafia gang. A 
cable T.V. operator controls a certain area and he exercises unquestionable 
monopoly. Though another operator offers  better and cheaper services, he is 
not permitted to step into that area. The monopolising operator fixes his own 
sen/ice charges, installation charge s and advance deposits, decides the 
channels, includes as many general and local advertisements as he wishes, 
and does things of his choice. The viewers feel helpless as there is no 
alternative. Sir, I think, it is high time  the Government of India took immediate 
measures to check these tendencies by id entifying an authority to control the 
activities of cable T.V. operators, which can introduce licence system, prescribe 
minimum technical qualifications to operators, demarcate the area of operation, 
fix monthly charges, ensure standard servic es with better quality and the like. 
Unless the monopolistic tendencies are curbed and a healthy spirit of 
competition is allowed, the viewers or  the consumers will continue to suffer 
silently. There must be a limit for ad vertisements on paid channels. I would 
appeal to the hon. Minister of Information and Broadcasting to give a serious 
thought to this problem and evolve an effective solution.
